whyThisMatters: Real security moments are fast. You do not get time to research if a link, a login, or a habit is safe. This game trains you to spot bad habits quickly. It also helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: Fast instinct is good. But some controls only sound safe, like a short password with symbols, old antivirus, or a public charging cable. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the 6 trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why "SMS Code Received" still counts as good, even though it sounds weaker than other MFA. What does "better than nothing" mean here?
Ask why a short password with symbols still looks strong to most people, and why that idea is wrong.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that looks related to security - like MFA, antivirus, or password - without checking if it is actually strong, current, or real. The 6 trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.note: This is still real MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication, a second check after your password). A text code is weaker than an app code because attackers can sometimes redirect your phone number to their own device and read the code. But it is far better than only a password. "Better than nothing" is a real upgrade.
A long random phrase without symbols can still be stronger than a short "complex" password. Length matters more than adding symbols.
Symbols do not save a short password. Length matters more than complexity. An 8-character password can be guessed quickly, no matter how it looks.
"Juice jacking" - a public USB port or cable can push harmful software or take data through the same link that charges your phone.
Authority plus urgency is the classic trick for Business Email Compromise. It is not proof that a request is real. It is designed to make you skip checks.
Antivirus that was installed last year and never updated does not help much against new threats. "Installed" is not the same as "up to date".
